    pushed.** With a gitlab.com URL (wink, 2026-08-21, `t1-vc-x1`) init built and committed
    both sides, then the push failed: GitLab does not create a project on push, so the
    remote was "not found" and the local tree was left behind for the user to delete.
    - **Cost:** no GitLab support in practice, and the leftover directory makes a rerun stop
      at preflight with "already exists".
    - **Fix direction:** provision the two projects before pushing, through the GitLab API or
      its CLI (`glab repo create`), as a gitlab.com arm beside the `gh` one. Rides the "Drop
      the global config and the account notion" Todo entry with #10.

  - The first proposal was a heuristic, reading `X/Y` as a path when `X` names an existing
    directory. wink's question, under what conditions `tmp/foo` is ambiguous, dissolved it: always,
    since nothing needs to exist for a path target (init creates missing parents), so both readings
    are well-formed for every such string and the heuristic guesses at intent rather than detecting
    anything.

content.text:
Grounding first: nothing in the repo currently links to `#todo` or `#bugs`, so this is a latent hazard rather than a live break. And `## Todo` is cited 16 times across `AGENTS.md`, `notes.md`, `prose.md`, and the backlog, all of which are the family's shared set.

**My thought: rename the titles, not the sections.** The collision is `# Todo` (line 1) against `## Todo` (the section), and the two sides cost very different amounts.

- Renaming the **section** touches those 16 citations, lands in the payload, and makes every adopter re-sync. It also renames a term the protocol speaks in prose constantly ("move the chosen `## Todo` entry into `## In Progress`"), and `Todo-list` or `Todo-current` would become a second spelling of a defined term, which [One spelling per term](agent-data/prose.md#one-spelling-per-term) pushes against.
- Renaming the **title** is one line per file, cited by nothing, and no agent-file text moves.

There is a second argument for the title being the thing that is wrong. `TODO.md` holds seven sections, of which Todo is one. Continuation notes, the running cycle's record, the closed one, Waiting, Ideas, and the Bugs pointer are the rest. `# Todo` under-describes the file, and the collision is the symptom. `notes/todo-backlog.md` shows the shape that works: titled `# Todo Backlog`, it carries a `## Todo` section with no collision, because its title is more specific than any of its sections.

So something like `# Todo and cycle record` for `TODO.md` and `# Bug list` for `notes/bugs.md`, both more accurate than what they say now, and the anchors stop colliding as a side effect. For `bugs.md` there is an even simpler option: drop its `## Bugs` heading entirely, since the file is nothing but bugs and no rule governs its internal shape.

**On sequencing**, if you want it: this is convention work, so its own cycle, and the shape ships in the payload, which means it wants to ride the **Copy the proposed set into the payload, and re-sync** entry when the family answers. Doing it before then would put one more diff between us and the members we just sent a proposal to.

Worth noticing on its own: the check found a latent defect in the family's own prescribed file shape on its first run over live records, which is a fair argument that it earns its place.

The plain version: the section name is expensive to change because the rules mention it everywhere, and the file's title is cheap and is also the part that is inaccurate. Retitling both files fixes the clash and reads better, and it belongs with the next payload sync rather than in this cycle.

**On README, you are right and my earlier advice does not survive contact with it.** I argued for deferring because one dead ToC line was not worth a 63-site semicolon sweep. That argument was entirely contingent on not touching the file at all. Once there is content that belongs there, we pay the sweep either way, and 63 sites is about the size of the 70-site backlog sweep this cycle already did in one rung. So the reason to defer is gone.

What is user-facing from this cycle and currently undocumented or wrong in README:

- `validate-anchors` exists and README does not mention it.
- `init` writes `.vc-config.md`, while four README rows still say `.vc-config.toml`.
- `init` and `clone` reject `owner/name` targets, and README's own examples still teach that spelling.
- `init` refuses a repo name ending `.git`.
- `vc-config-model.md` exists at the repo root and is what a new member seeds from.
- The three `agent-session` keys are work-side only, which the resolution-order section states.

**The shape I would give a first cut**, so it does not fight the entry that will rewrite the file: prose and examples, no new flag table. `validate-anchors` has one positional and no flags, so there is nothing to table anyway, which means the new section is naturally already in the shape **CLI reference lives in `--help`, and README owns concepts** wants. A section the size of `validate-todo`'s, about fifteen lines, plus the corrections above, plus the conversion the touch obliges.

The one caution: this should document what changed and delete nothing else. Deleting the flag tables and the `## Usage` block is that entry's cycle, and folding it in here would quietly swallow a ranked entry.

Sequencing, if you want it: its own rung after this one and before the closing, something like **docs: README covers the new surface**. That also lets this rung stay what it is, and keeps the README diff, most of which is a mechanical sweep, out of the checker's diff.

The plain version: you are right that the README needs a first cut, and my reason for putting it off only held while we were not touching the file. It should be its own rung, adding a short section for the new command and correcting what init now writes, without starting the bigger README rewrite that is already queued.

**Repo set resolution.** `-R` and `--scope` compose:

1. Neither: workspace-default scope, `work,agent` if `repos.agent` is non-empty, else `work`. POR (no
   `.vc-config.toml`) -> `work` resolved to cwd.
2. `-R PATH` alone: sync just the repo at `PATH`.
3. `--scope=work|bot|work,bot` alone: workspace roles, resolved via the discovered workspace root's
   `.vc-config.toml` (`work` -> root, `agent` -> the root-joined `agent` path).
4. `-R PATH --scope=ROLES`: roles resolved against `PATH` as the workspace root.

Scope is cwd-portable: from `.claude/`, `vc-x1 sync` walks up to the workspace root and resolves
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqo   # points to a .claude repo change
ochid: /wtpmottv            # points to an work repo change
```

Paths always start with `/` (the workspace root, i.e. vc-x1). Each repo has a `.vc-config.toml` that
identifies its location within the workspace, so tools can resolve these paths locally.

For full details see:
- [Git trailer convention](./notes/chores/chores-01.md#git-trailer-convention)
```bash
find "${VC_X1_TEST_TMPDIR:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}}" -maxdepth 1 \
     -name 'vc-x1-*test*' -mtime +1 -exec rm -rf {} +
```

Requires `jj` to be installed. The `.claude` bot repo is cloned automatically via `git submodule` if
the source project was created with `vc-x1 init`.

    ../vc-x1-work-repo-template,../vc-x1-bot-repo-template

content.content:
### vc-config.md (the schema prototype)

[vc-config.md](vc-config.md) at the repo root (no leading dot) is the single source of truth for
the settable-key schema above, and at the same time its long-form documentation. It is not a
config file: one `##` section per settable key holds that key's prose and, in a `toml` fence,
that key's metadata, and build.rs parses the file and generates the schema table plus the
built-in default constants the binary compiles against. One file drives every surface:

- the `config` subcommand's printed schema (above)
- the commented blocks `init` writes into a new workspace's instance config
- the built-in defaults themselves (e.g. `agent-session --col-width`'s 68), consumed from the
  generated constants, so behavior cannot disagree with documentation
- each key's `reference:` url, so a reader of any generated config can click through to that
  key's own section

The file is read in the same format as an instance config: the `toml` fences, concatenated in
document order, form the TOML, and build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
loader. Prose between fences is documentation and never reaches a parser.

References are derived, not written: build.rs joins the single `[vc-config] reference-base` (the
bare repo url) with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#` and each key's heading anchor, so links follow the
repo's default branch and no branch name is baked in; the test suite fails if a key has no
matching heading. A per-key `reference` entry overrides the derivation for the odd key documented
elsewhere. A fork customizes both in one place: point `reference-base` at your repo and edit your
own copy of the file.

lastPrompt: How about some stats on the number of links checked with pass/fail count, also -v and -vv should output information about each site. Thoughts only

content.text:
Agreed on both, and the first one is a real gap rather than a nicety.

**The denominator is wrong today.** The summary says `40 files checked, 9 problem(s) found`, so a file with no links passes exactly like a file with four hundred. A silent pass and a vacuous pass are indistinguishable, which is the same complaint bug #9 makes about `config --validate` mixing "checked, found nothing" with "could not check". Counting the checks rather than the files fixes it, and everything needed is already computed and then thrown away: `anchor_targets` walks every target and only the failures survive.

**What is worth counting**, and one of these matters more than the rest:

- anchor targets resolved, passed and failed
- reference numbers paired, cited and defined
- headings slugged, and the duplicates among them
- **cross-file targets skipped**

The last one is the interesting number. It is precisely the coverage this rung does not have, and it is the metric that goes to zero when the cross-file stretch lands. Printing it makes the gap visible instead of leaving a reader to assume every link was checked. Something like:

```
validate-anchors: 40 files, 612 links checked, 9 failed, 47 cross-file skipped
```

**On the verbosity layering**, `-v` is Debug and `-vv` is Trace here, both to stderr, so the natural split is:

- default: the findings and the summary, as now
- `-v`: one line per file with its own counts, so coverage is visible per file rather than only in aggregate
- `-vv`: one line per site. Every target with how it resolved (ok, cross-file skipped, failed), every reference pairing, and every heading with the slug it produced

That last part earns its place beyond debugging the tool. The slug algorithm is subtle enough that `a + b` becomes `a--b` while `a: b` becomes `a-b`, so when a link fails the question is always "what did that heading actually slug to", and `-vv` answers it directly.

**One more, cheap and probably the most useful of all.** When a target fails, the tool knows every slug in the file, so it can name the nearest one: `'#todo-format' matches no heading. Did you mean '#todo-format-shape'?` That converts a finding into a fix without the reader opening the file. It is a few lines of edit distance over a list that is already in hand.

**Where it lands.** Its own rung after this one, since the README rung in flight is finished and this is a different subject. Worth knowing that it will want two lines of README touch-up, because the section I just wrote describes the output. That is cheap now rather than expensive, since the semicolon sweep is already paid on that file, which is a small argument for doing the stats soon rather than later.

The plain version: right now the tool says how many files it looked at, not how many links, so "all links resolve" could mean it checked hundreds or none. Counting links, and showing how many it deliberately skipped, tells the truth about what was covered. `-v` should break that down per file and `-vv` per link, and while we are in there, a failing link should suggest the closest heading it could have meant.

content.content:
### validate-anchors

Check a markdown record's own links, so a dead anchor is found by a command rather than by a
reader. Three checks, all within one file:

- every `](#slug)` link and `[N]: #slug` definition resolves to a heading in the same file
- every `[[N]]` citation has an `[N]:` definition, and every definition is cited, counting the
  `[text][N]` reference-link form a ladder rung uses for its own subsection
- no two headings slug to the same anchor, which markdown resolves silently, so every link to it
  reaches the first heading

Cross-file targets (`](other.md#slug)`) are recognized and skipped, since resolving one means
slugging another file. Read-only, and exits non-zero when anything is found.

```
# Every markdown record in the workspace
vc-x1 validate-anchors

# Specific files, which is also how the frozen history is checked,
# since notes/chores/ and notes/done.md are out of the default set
vc-x1 validate-anchors TODO.md notes/bugs.md
```

The slug algorithm is the one [notes.md](./agent-data/notes.md#markdown-anchor-links) documents:
lowercase, drop every character that is not alphanumeric, a hyphen, or an underscore, and map each
remaining space to one hyphen. Adjacent spaces are not collapsed, so `a + b` becomes `a--b` while
`a: b` becomes `a-b`.

### validate

**On the rename, yes, and I would push the name one step further than you did.**

The case for moving it out of `config --validate` is strong. The family is `validate-desc`, `validate-todo`, `validate-agent`, `validate-anchors`, and the config check is the only one hiding behind another subcommand's flag. **The validate family: umbrella, runner, and `validate-work`** plans a bare `validate` that runs everything applying to the workspace, "each reported by name" — every sibling slots in, while `config --validate` needs special-casing. And `config`'s own job is printing the schema, which is a different verb from checking a file against it.

Where I would differ is `vc-` in the name. Every sibling is `validate-<object>` with a short common noun, and the object here includes the user config at `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`, which is plain TOML and not a vc-config file at all — the same code checks it today when you pass its path. `validate-vc-config` names a format and would then be wrong about one of the things it validates, where `validate-config` names the object and stays true. The `vc-` is already carried by the binary.

So my suggestion is `validate-config`, with `validate-vc-config` the better choice only if you want the command scoped to the vc-config format and the user config handled elsewhere.

**Cost, which is small but not nothing.** It is a CLI surface change, so `config --validate` gets the rejection-with-fix-it treatment that `bot-session` and the legacy `[workspace]` schema got. README's config section loses the flag and gains a sibling section. And **The validate family** needs a line saying this slice landed early, since that entry currently says `validate-work` will call `config --validate`.

**Sequencing.** Its own rung in this cycle, next. Doing it now is meaningfully cheaper than later: the code is open, and the README section written two rungs ago documents a spelling we would otherwise ship and immediately retire. Same pattern as taking the `owner/name` slice out of **Drop the global config** early.
